content: In departments or clinics where tuberculosis (TB) services are provided, or in laboratory and radiology departments, one healthcare worker from each cadre involved in the testing or service output should be asked to describe the entire process. This includes identifying all staff involved, the time required, and the supplies and equipment used, where applicable. At least one method of staff time measurement (e.g., interview, observation, or timesheet) must be captured for every service output. The data collection sheets have been formatted to allow data to be collected either electronically (entered directly into the Data Collection Sheets) or on hard copies (recorded on printed sheets). The method of data collection should be chosen based on what is most suitable for the facility. It is recommended to use all three methods of staff time measurement (interviews, observations, and timesheets) for each service output, as the staff cost component of unit costs derived by each method will be compared during analysis. However, if this is not feasible, at least one methodology must be applied to each service output. A supply wastage proportion assumption must be documented. For example, based on the Value TB study, the wastage proportion for Xpert® MTB/RIF was estimated at 3–5%. Informed consent forms must be provided to every individual from whom data is collected via interviews, observations, or timesheets. These forms should be stored securely, and a dropdown option in the tool should indicate whether consent has been obtained. All staff time measures (interviews, observations, and timesheets) should be applied to at least one healthcare worker in each cadre involved in every service output. If it is not possible to administer all three methods to each healthcare worker, ensure that at least one method is used to measure their time. Information on the utilization of TB-related services within the health facility, such as the annual number of outpatient and community visits, should be collected and entered into the relevant sheet. A breakdown of top-down and bottom-up quantities is also provided. For example, for drugs, top-down quantities refer to the total amount of each TB medication dispensed within the facility, while bottom-up quantities refer to sampled usage by patients. The staff-time interview template is one method used to capture the quantity and allocation of staff time. The second method involves weekly timesheet templates, which can be printed and distributed to staff members at the beginning of the data collection week and collected at the end. For example, the total staff time for a chest X-ray would include the time spent taking the X-ray, reading and interpreting the results, and documenting them. The data sheet includes an exhaustive list of supplies (primarily laboratory supplies and infection control materials) used for TB services at a facility, with prices collected as mentioned. For each supply category, the annual expenditure and percentage use for TB services will be documented. Wastage of supplies refers to the percentage of supplies discarded due to expiration or other reasons. If the wastage value for the facility cannot be obtained, an estimated value for the country can be used. The equipment price list should be collected centrally and used for each facility. If the prices paid for the equipment are known, they should be adjusted for inflation using the Consumer Price Index (CPI) and converted to USD using the exchange rate of the relevant year. The most appropriate value for the unit price is the replacement cost. The Data Entry Tool is used for data analysis at the facility level to generate bottom-up and top-down unit costs. Once finalized, the Data Entry Tools for each facility should be securely stored and shared with study investigators for pooled analysis. The tool allows data analysts to clean and review the collected data and examine the components and methods used to calculate unit costs. It provides calculations and links that summarize cost data by service outputs in capital and recurrent categories and by intervention type for TB services, laboratory, and radiology tests. These datasets can be explored in Excel or exported into statistical software such as STATA or R Studio for pooled analysis. Data should be transferred from the Data Collection Tool to the Data Entry Tool by pasting values or values with number formatting only, ensuring that cell formats are not altered and that there are no links to other files. Identical sheets in the Data Collection and Data Entry Tools should be copied as described. The estimated time for transferring data from the Data Collection Tool into the Data Entry Tool, including data management and validation, is approximately one day for smaller facilities and up to three days for larger facilities. The glossary defines the acronyms and abbreviations used within the tool. Instructions describe the color-coding of the sheets and cells in the tool and how they should be used. The source of all data must be provided, whether from a specific agency, website, established methodology, or assumption. The useful life values for equipment can be obtained from WHO CHOICE or other relevant sources.
